summary: Loss Aversion (Kahneman & Tversky): Pain of losing is psychologically twice as powerful as pleasure of gaining, making perceived quality risks in online purchases a major barrier.
notes: High relevance to non-perishable/fresh category trial.

summary: Social Proof (Cialdini): People look to actions and recommendations of others when uncertain about a purchase decision in unfamiliar categories.
Choice Overload & Decision Fatigue (Iyengar & Lepper): Excessive options increase cognitive effort and abandonment, requiring curated trust signals.
source: Iyengar & Lepper (2000) When Choice is Demotivating
notes: Reduces friction in broad catalog navigation.

summary: Perceived Risk Reduction Theory (Bauer): Consumers actively employ risk-reduction strategies (e.g. guarantees, reviews) when evaluating unknown online sellers or product lines.
source: Bauer (1960) Consumer Behavior as Risk Taking

summary: Trust Signals Theory (Fukuyama/Bachmann): Explicit institutional or platform commitments build trust in high-uncertainty transactions.
Habit Formation & Loop Model (Wood & Neal): Repeated friction-free experiences turn deliberate shopping behaviors into automatic routine purchases.
Switching Costs Theory (Burnham et al.): High cognitive or financial switching costs prevent customers from migrating to alternative platforms when issues arise.
source: Burnham et al. (2003) Consumer Switching Costs
notes: Explains churn following bad resolution experiences.

summary: Mental Accounting (Thaler): Consumers frame transactions into distinct mental accounts, treating unexpected losses (bad items) differently than planned spend.
source: Thaler (1985) Mental Accounting and Consumer Choice

summary: Default Bias & Status Quo Bias (Samuelson & Zeckhauser): Users default to familiar categories unless friction-free trial cues alter the baseline behavior.
source: Samuelson & Zeckhauser (1988) Status Quo Bias in Decision Making

summary: Peak-End Rule (Kahneman): Customer memory of an experience is dominated by its emotional peak and its final resolution, making post-purchase support decisive.
source: Kahneman et al. (1993) When More Pain Is Preferred

summary: Availability Bias (Tversky & Kahneman): Vivid memories of single negative experiences (e.g. rotten produce) heavily distort subsequent likelihood estimates of quality.
notes: Explains outsized impact of bad initial deliveries.

summary: Confirmation Bias (Nickerson): Customers expecting low quality in new online categories selectively focus on negative cues unless counter-evidence is prominent.
Uncertainty Reduction Theory (Berger & Calabrese): Consumers seek explicit information and operational transparency to lower anxiety during novelty.
Endowment Effect (Kahneman et al.): Ownership increases valuation; providing instant compensation restores sense of rightful ownership upon delivery defects.
Cognitive Dissonance Theory (Festinger): Post-purchase anxiety after buying an unfamiliar item is mitigated by immediate positive reinforcement and easy returns.
notes: Addresses buyer remorse in new categories.

summary: Bandwagon Effect (Leibenstein): Demand for goods increases when consumers perceive that others are actively adopting and trusting the product line.
column9: Validates popularity badges for category trial.

summary: Framing Effect (Tversky & Kahneman): Presenting quality guarantees in terms of zero risk or 100% replacement alters customer risk perception positively.
Sunk Cost Fallacy (Arkes & Blumer): Subscription or loyalty membership investments increase willingness to try secondary categories within the same app.
source: Arkes & Blumer (1985) Psychology of Sunk Cost
notes: Relevant for quick commerce loyalty programs.

summary: Signaling Theory (Spence): High-quality sellers use costly or explicit signals (e.g., freshness guarantees) that low-quality sellers cannot credibly match.
Hick-Hyman Law: Time to make a decision increases logarithmically with the number of options, favoring structured category presentation.
source: Hick (1952) On the Rate of Gain of Information
notes: Improves navigation and category entry speed.

summary: Scarcity Principle (Cialdini): Perceived limited availability of fresh batch items increases perceived value and urgency of purchase.
Initial Trust Formation Model (McKnight et al.): Initial trust in an e-commerce platform relies on structural assurances (guarantees) and perceived site reputation.
source: McKnight et al. (2002) Initial Trust in E-Commerce

summary: Expectation-Confirmation Theory (Bhattacherjee): Re-purchase intention is governed by whether post-purchase performance matches pre-purchase expectations.
Hyperbolic Discounting (Laibson): Customers overvalue immediate delivery gratification, making fulfillment delays or errors disproportionately painful.
source: Laibson (1997) Golden Eggs and Hyperbolic Discounting

summary: Authority Bias (Milgram): Recommendations from certified experts or quality badges significantly reduce purchase hesitation for sensitive items.
notes: Applies to personal care and baby products.
